document.title: Afghanistan: Taliban Said to Loosen Grip on Bin Ladin as They Increasingly Turn to Him for Financial Support and Advice (Islamabad 04450)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Haqqani History: Bin Ladin's Advocate Inside the Taliban
document.note: [Confidential] Sources say Jalaluddin Haqqani is an important advocate for Osama bin Laden within the Taliban administration. Bin Laden appears to operate largely free of Taliban control and to be protected by Taliban elements. His growing autonomy is attributed to the strength of supporters such as Haqqani, who are ideologically close to him and have argued for reducing controls on him.

events.description: Taliban captured Nangarhar Province, where bin Ladin was living; start of Taliban/bin Ladin relationship.

Bin Ladin held a press conference in Khost.
Taliban envoy Abdul Hakim Mujahid told POLOFF Taliban had no prior knowledge of the press conference and had lectured bin Ladin.
US Embassy Islamabad cable reports Taliban increasingly seeking bin Ladin's money and advice.
Taliban captured Nangarhar province, where bin Ladin was living, beginning the Taliban/bin Ladin relationship.
Bin Ladin fled Sudan in mid-1996 and went to Nangarhar.

US Embassy Islamabad cable (Islamabad 04450, signed Simons) assesses that the Taliban are loosening their grip on bin Ladin and increasingly turning to him for financial support and advice; the relationship may be growing closer.

sources_cited: Confidential US Embassy sources met by POLOFF on 10, 11 and 12 June 1998
Bin Ladin's 26 May 1998 press conference and ABC News interview
key_claims: The Taliban increasingly requested bin Ladin funding for arms, salaries and communications equipment before the 1998 fighting season.
Bin Ladin reportedly provided more money in 1998 than in 1996-97.
The Taliban-bin Ladin relationship dates from September 1996 when the Taliban took Nangarhar.
Bin Ladin is not in the Taliban's all-Afghan inner circle and is not fully trusted.
Sources speculate a quid pro quo: hosting and greater freedom of movement in return for financial assistance.
Jalaluddin Haqqani, Syed Abdullah and Abdul Kabir are said to be ideologically close to bin Ladin and to have argued for loosening controls on him.
Taliban leaders such as Mullah Hassan and Jalil reportedly sought his advice on dealing with the UN and West.
